content.title: Signal restricts mobile screenshots as it confronts ‘existential threat’ of AI surveillance
content.text: Signal restricts mobile screenshots as it confronts ‘existential threat’ of AI surveillance | TechCrunch In Brief Posted: 1:37 PM PST · November 21, 2026 Image Credits: Matthias Balk/picture alliance / Getty Images Anthony Ha Signal restricts mobile screenshots as it confronts ‘existential threat’ of AI surveillance Signal announced Friday that it’s limiting users’ ability to take screenshots within the secure messaging app — a response to what President Meredith Whittaker described as the “existential threat” of operating systems that integrate agentic AI. Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability to “scan” the information on users’ screens, Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS “are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.” “Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” she said. “All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.” Signal already sought to limit these risks by blocking screenshots of its Windows app by default. Now it’s adding similar restrictions in Android and iOS. That said, users can disable this setting if they wish, which Whittaker said would “break our privacy guarantees.” She also admitted this is an “incomplete” solution, as it doesn’t “address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data.” Topics AI , Apps , Meredith Whittaker , Security , signal , Social 2027 San Francisco Get an Early Peek at the Next TechCrunch Disrupt Disrupt, Startup Battlefield, and more will return next year, and you can be at the front of the line. content.title: A tale of two Nvidias
content.text: A tale of two Nvidias | TechCrunch Image Credits: Fabrice COFFRINI/AFP / Getty Images AI A tale of two Nvidias Anthony Ha 1:07 PM PST · November 21, 2026 Listen on Apple Podcasts Listen on Spotify We got two very different pictures of Nvidia this week, depending on whether you were focused on the company’s latest earnings report or the tech executives loudly calling for former CEO Jensen Huang’s return. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Tim De Chant, and I discussed the latest news from the AI chipmaker, which reported soaring revenue and insisted that it has no plans for Huang to return. Kirsten described this as “the tale of two Nvidias this week,” with the company’s current executives assuring investors, “Hey, we’ve got this.” At the same time, “You’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back , circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back.” (The company’s falling stock price certainly suggests that Wall Street isn’t feeling reassured.) Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity. Kirsten Korosec: Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China . This was coming directly from the interim CEO Colette Kress, and that coincides with the Trump administration also talking about closing off what we have discussed in the past, which is this idea of remote access — really closing and tightening all these restrictions [so] the chips can’t make it into China. What was happening is that data centers were being set up right outside, in countries like Malaysia and elsewhere, and then companies within China were remote accessing these chips, and so that’s now also been shut down. A lot is happening on the China front that is so much bigger than Nvidia, but Nvidia came out publicly and said, “Nope, we’re shutting this part down.” I’ll be very curious to see if this changes, maybe in the first half of 2027. Tim De Chant: I’d love to be a fly on the wall in some of these Trump administration conversations, because they were much more stringent in terms of export controls at the end of the first Trump administration, and that continued through the Biden administration, where they really restricted Nvidia’s ability to export chips to China. I think that something changed in the last couple of years that really opened Nvidia’s ability to sell in the country. Anthony Ha: One of the things that really surprised me as we were preparing for this episode was [learning that critics] of Nvidia’s stance towards China estimate that 20% of their business comes from China. And again, that’s not something you’re going to see directly in their financials, because that’s not direct sales to Chinese companies. But they’re saying, “A lot of the chips that are getting sold to companies in Malaysia or other companies in East Asia or Southeast Asia are going to end up [used by companies in] China eventually.” And so that could be — if Nvidia is really serious about this, I think this is something that’s very much in flux — that could actually be a pretty significant blow to their bottom line. Kirsten: Although Nvidia’s bottom line is doing just fine. In every possible way, their guidance was incredible. They beat expectations. They have a long pipeline. It was really interesting because you have that happening, and then you have all this noise happening in social media, and also a number of other tech conferences were happening this past week — Dealbook Summit, there [were] a few others in which you had the highest profile people that you can think of in the tech world commenting on Jensen [Huang], and Jensen himself commenting. So it’s like the tale of two Nvidias this week. You’ve got the earnings and the current executives really talking about, “Hey, we’ve got this.” In fact, that was the last line that Collette Kress said [on the earnings call]. And then at the exact same time, or in parallel, you’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back, circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back. So it’s really quite the drama that we are definitely not done with, by the way. Anthony: Although I think that what the folks who’d like to see Jensen Huang come back would say is that this most recent quarter is the last quarter under him. This is the [last of the] good times that we’re seeing under him. And so we don’t know how well Nvidia will do without him. It seems like Nvidia’s public stance right now [on Huang’s possible return] is, “No, that’s not happening.” But Nvidia’s public stance a week and a half before that was, “We stand behind Jensen. We have every confidence in his leadership.” So depending on the various pressures on them, you can imagine that changing. I don’t know what it would take for that to happen. I don’t necessarily think it’s that likely, but I also don’t think that just because they’re saying it’s not happening now doesn’t mean it will never happen. Kirsten: Sure, never say never. Tim: Right, never say never. I do think that to some extent, their steadfastness and how quickly they shot down the petitions asking for Jensen to return suggests there’s maybe a little bit more going on behind the scenes than we know on the outside. So that’s probably something to watch in the coming weeks. Kirsten: I think that the board is trying to be in control here, and they don’t want to be forced into a decision because someone like Elon Musk is saying that it needs to happen. And so, even if there is a day in which Jensen returns — which I think is pretty unlikely, especially because the investigation into how much and who knew what about chips being sold, allegedly, secretly to China. We don’t know the full picture of that yet. But even if they did have the full picture, they want to present control, and they definitely don’t want to appear like they have deference to some other tech billionaire out there. Tim: I’m sure they’re looking at what happened at OpenAI and not wanting to repeat that. Anthony: I imagine the dynamic’s a little bit different, since Nvidia is a public company. So, I’m not an expert on this, but I would guess it would be much harder for you Jensen Huang to come back and just toss out a bunch of board members. content.text: Here are the top AI agents that can live in your text messages  | TechCrunch Image Credits: Tero Vesalainen / Getty Images AI Here are the top AI agents that can live in your text messages Lauren Forristal 9:00 AM PST · November 21, 2026 Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person. You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later. While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present, thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space. Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work. Ask Proxy Image Credits: Ask Proxy Ask Proxy ’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the company explains on its website. It works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add important dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. You can also send it photos, like an empty table, to figure out how to decorate the table for a dinner party. Unlike a typical chatbot, Ask Proxy also takes a proactive approach. It can reach out when it notices something you might forget or when it comes across a new activity, restaurant, or experience you might enjoy. There’s also a work-focused version, which the company explains “gets employees back to work faster, while keeping personal data off company systems.” The personal version costs $1 per day. For businesses, pricing starts at $15 per employee per month for large companies and $23 per employee per month for small teams with fewer than 49 employees. Ask Proxy works over SMS. You can text “start” to 820-732-2625. Caddy Image Credits: Caddy Caddy is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check. For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you. Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026. Comma Image Credits: Comma Comma is designed to manage tasks across both work and everyday life. Comma carries tasks through to completion, checking its own work and determining when a task is finished. Completed work is surfaced for review when a decision or approval is needed. It also proactively notifies users and recommends the next steps. It can work across a user’s browser, computer, and files, while remaining accessible remotely through messaging apps such as Signal, Telegram, and WeChat. Comma maintains context and memory across devices and conversations, and can deliver daily briefings, flag urgent matters, and summarize recorded calls. Comma is free to start and open source. Fambot Image Credits: Fambot Fambot is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan. The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar. Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future. The company launched in beta in early September 2026 and has raised $3.5 million in pre-seed funding. The service is currently free during the beta period, but Fambot expects to eventually charge roughly the equivalent of a Netflix subscription. Folk Image Credits: Folk Folk is designed to be an AI assistant you can reach through iMessage, WhatsApp, and Telegram. It can remember personal context, manage reminders, research topics, track flights, handle email, and perform real-world tasks such as restaurant reservations. One distinction is that Folk runs on its own private cloud computer. It can also run code and execute multi-step tasks rather than merely responding conversationally. Folk launched its beta in May 2026, and it’s available for free but also offers a Pro subscription for $8.33/month if you want unlimited tasks running in the background. Haven Image Credits: Haven Haven distinguishes itself by presenting the concept of a “digital twin” rather than merely serving as a text-based AI assistant. According to the company, Haven understands and adapts to your preferences, routines, and decision-making styles, creating a personalized memory graph based on your interactions. As the company describes , “A personal assistant knows what you asked it to do. Haven knows what you would do and how you would do it.” Notably, the company envisions future features that customize your experiences across devices, like TV and car. Currently, Haven is available for free in beta on iPhone and Android devices, and the web. You can also reach Haven by calling or texting (435) 260-6500. Instinct Image Credits: Instinct Instinct first made headlines after raising $350 million at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised $1 billion , valuing it at $10 billion. The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions. In September, Instinct began giving users dedicated email addresses for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account. (However, this level of autonomy has also raised concerns about privacy and security .) It’s also begun rolling out support for placing calls . The company remains in private beta. Iris Image Credits: Iris Powered by Hermes Agent, Iris is designed to let users delegate tasks to an AI assistant directly through iMessage. Users can connect the apps they use and hand over a task with a simple message. The agent then works through the required steps, while retaining relevant context from previous interactions. It’s also designed to follow up with users proactively rather than waiting for another request. Martin Image Credits: Martin Martin is a general-purpose personal assistant reachable through SMS as well as phone, WhatsApp, email, Slack, and its own iOS app. It can help manage calendars, email, reminders, tasks, notes, and communications. content.title: Is selling an AI version of your face to this microdrama startup the future of Hollywood?
content.text: Is selling an AI version of your face to this microdrama startup the future of Hollywood? | TechCrunch Image Credits: Shortical AI Is selling an AI version of your face to this microdrama startup the future of Hollywood? Lucas Ropek 8:00 AM PST · November 21, 2026 For the most part, the content offered by the microdrama startup Shortical is indistinguishable from the rest of its industry . The company produces soapy, melodramatic storylines — almost always risqué romances — that, in bite-sized two-minute episodes, compel viewers to stay glued to their phones so as not to miss the latest twist in a tawdry, cliff-hanger-happy saga. The primary way that Shortical — which was founded last January — makes money is through subscriptions. Typically, the first 7-10 episodes of a micro-drama are free. After that, if the user wants to finish the series, they have to pay a small monthly fee which unlocks access to all of the site’s content. Over the past year, the company has churned out a gush of popular live-action romances like “Crossing the Line with My Neighbor,” “Accidentally Married My Boss,” and “Spoiled by My Billionaire Sugar Daddy.” Lately, however, the company’s homepage is covered in AI-generated content. The reason isn’t exactly hard to figure out: the production overhead for AI content is substantially less than live-action. The profit potential, meanwhile, is substantially higher, if you can draw an audience. Its latest microdrama premiered in Los Angeles last week. The series, called “Inevitable,” stars Aki Avni, an Israeli film and television star who has been visible in American TV shows for years (he had a stint on Fox’s 9/11-era thriller “24” years ago) but is now trying something largely unheard of in modern Hollywood: licensing his face to Shortical for the sake of its AI content. The project, which is wholly AI, used Avni’s face to create a digital avatar of him. In “Inevitable,” he plays himself – in a very meta plot in which he — the actor Aki Avni — licenses his face to a film studio, after which thriller-like antics ensue. This is Shortical’s first foray into such a licensing deal, but it likely won’t be their last. In a phone interview, Avni told TechCrunch that he found the project both nerveracking and exciting. “Look, it’s a new era for artists,” the actor said. “AI is a new kind of art. It’s a new format. It’s always great to be the pioneer in something.” Guy Shimoni, the CEO of Shortical, emphasized the creative potential of the new tool. “One of the things that AI does is it enables smaller teams to be able to produce these movie-scale productions,” Shimoni said. “When we were doing mobile-first live action, we were limited by budget, but now we can serve them with epic fantasies. We have kingdoms and dragons. We have superheroes. We have werewolves.” But AI-generated romances involving werewolves — who, exactly, is watching this kind of thing? Apparently, a lot of people. While China boasts the biggest microdrama audience globally, Shimoni says that most of his platform’s viewers are actually in the U.S. The industry’s viewer demographic skews heavily female . Many viewers may watch them to wind down at night , getting minor dopamine hits as they drift off to sleep. Many of the AI-generated programs that already exist on the company’s website appear to have millions of views. Now, Shortical is betting on the creation of a new generation of creators — those who, like Avni, are willing to surrender their likenesses for compensation. “ LICENSE YOUR FACE ” Shortical’s website advertises, explaining that interested parties can submit their social media handles to the company, which will then decide whether to offer them “a contract setting out the terms” of using their persona in the company’s AI-generated content. A company rep told TechCrunch that this “offering is still in its early days and hasn’t yet resulted in any signed contracts.” They added: “The series with Aki is the first time Shortical has used a real person’s likeness, and it was done through a direct agreement with him rather than through the platform. Shortical hopes the series will draw more attention to face licensing and plans to promote the offering more actively following this launch.” Much of this trend has already taken hold in China where the microdrama industry originated, where AI-generated content is big, and where face-licensing is already a trend. Although the trend may not be a particularly profitable one for creators. A recent report in Rest of World found that Microdrama firms were paying people “between US$15 to US$700 to license their facial likenesses.” How much money is Shortical offering for its face-licensing deals? The company isn’t saying. As for if Shortical will offer royalty-based compensation for creators — like the residual system in television, “It’s a case by case [basis],” Shimoni answers vaguely. A Shortical representative further explained to TechCrunch that the company didn’t want to “share a specific figure” for Avni’s particular contract. However, the person said, he came “on as a partner in the project, and his compensation was in line with industry standards for a comparable non-AI acting role.” For other actors, however, the deals may be quite different. Plus, many creatives are understandably unsettled by signs of automation creeping into their industry. Until recently, microdramas seemed like a safe, entry-level gateway into the entertainment industry, where young actors could gain experience on sets and hone their craft. Now, companies are downsizing and producing content that doesn’t even require real actors. Jennifer Cooper, a longtime fan of the industry and founder of the consultancy firm Vertical Drama Love, notes that there’s a lot of distrust of AI — both from audiences and within the microdrama industry itself. “Everyone’s been impacted by AI,” she said. “A lot of us have either lost work to AI or can see that it’s devastated this industry — [taking microdramas] from something that was a rare thing in the world, that was in growth, and providing work, particularly for young people…[and now] you know, it’s been decimated.” Questions of consent with AI likenesses have also dogged the industry (some creators claim they have had their likenesses stolen ), which is something that Shortical is obviously trying to address with its new face-licensing endeavor. Yet these licensing deals could also help to gig-ify the industry, creating a scenario in which creators pay a distributor for the chance to platform their content (or their face), then receive payouts based on the audience engagement they’re allowed to generate. Shortical recently partnered with a company called Payouts.com, which describes itself as a “payout infrastructure platform powering creator and gig economy disbursements at scale.” The plan is to create a system by which creatives can seamlessly interact with Shortical’s platform and get paid. Cooper believes the push towards AI in the industry is driven by broader financial trends. Most of the microdrama business is led by startups, and VCs love to hear a growth game plan involving automation. “For anyone to get investment at the moment in microdramas, they’ve got to mention the word AI,” she says. “It’s like AI equals gold in everyone’s eyes.” Despite all the investment in this space, Cooper seems skeptical that there is actually a huge audience for this kind of content. “Some of it does get views. A lot of it doesn’t,” she said, of the AI content. “I think it’s being pushed on an audience more than there is an audience demand or wish for it.” Topics AI , AI , entertainment , Hollywood , Media & Entertainment , microdramas When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . Countries agree to ‘start discussing options’ for rules around autonomous weapons. by Terrence O'Brien Nov 21, 2026, 8:03 PM UTC Link Share Gift Photo by John Moore/Getty Images Terrence O'Brien is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths. One of the items on the agenda for UN diplomats meeting in Geneva this week was working towards rules regarding the use of autonomous weapons, or so-called “killer robots.” Eventually, representatives left the meetings agreeing to “start discussing options” after a largely fruitless week of negotiations. According to NPR : Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo. The compromise reached was that countries would instead have two years to propose regulations. Negotiations between countries on which regulations to adopt and how to enforce them will likely drag on well beyond that. Additionally, room was left for some of those yet-to-be-adopted regulations to remain “optional.” Humanitarian organizations and some countries see a need to urgently adopt legally binding rules as semi-autonomous weapons and drones have been responsible for a significant number of civilian deaths in conflicts around the globe, including in Ukraine , Gaza , and Sudan. According to NPR , Russia, Israel, and the US proved to be the primary obstructions: On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting’s agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons. The Anthropic IPO raises big questions about the future of AI, the company’s safety-first mission, and how we balance idealism with capitalism. by Nilay Patel Nov 21, 2026, 3:00 PM UTC Link Share Nilay Patel is editor-in-chief of The Verge, host of the Decoder podcast , and co-host of The Vergecast . Today, I’m talking with Hayden Field, The Verge ’s senior AI reporter, about the Anthropic IPO for the third and final episode in our series about AI in real life. The AI lab behind Claude went public on the Nasdaq last Thursday. The numbers are gigantic, but not really that important for this conversation, except to say that Anthropic has become one of the most valuable companies on the planet. The real story is what happens now — and whether Anthropic can continue to thread the needle of caring about and investing in AI safety while also being a public company beholden to shareholders. Oh, and it also continuously growing the amount of money it makes so it can keep paying its ever-increasing compute bills, which total roughly $900 billion over the coming years. All of these ideas sit in a fascinating tension with one another, and so Hayden and I really tried to break down how we think this might play out as Anthropic navigates the pressures of the public markets. You’ll hear us talk about the company’s unique corporate governance structure , something that is especially relevant in the wake of the ongoing Jensen Huang saga. We also get into why OpenAI seems happy to have let Anthropic go public first , and why Anthropic’s whole pitch to big customers boils down to the same safety branding that now sits in conflict with the profit-oriented part of its business. Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday. Okay: Hayden Field, The Verge ’s senior AI reporter, on the Anthropic IPO and the economics of frontier AI. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Hayden Field, welcome back to Decoder . Thanks. Great to be here. I’m excited to talk to you today because it’s not pure soap opera drama chaos. I know. It’s like a normal thing that happened. It’s for once not personality-based and soap opera. It’s about cold, hard would-be cash. [Laughs] Well, there is some personality in it because we’re going to talk a lot about Anthropic’s IPO, which has a bunch of big personalities in it, and the way they have structured this company to repel the rapacious pressures of capitalism is, I would say, very eccentric. It reflects the beliefs of a number of eccentric people. Yep, absolutely. It’s really been interesting digging into the S-1 again and just seeing who was on what committee and which founders have the most control here and how much control the founders actually have, which is more than it may seem. Gaming AI Entertainment Chess.com’s next move is a new hub for classic games, from mahjong to sudoku AI changed the game at Chess.com, helping it expand to 11 other classics this year.﻿ AI changed the game at Chess.com, helping it expand to 11 other classics this year.﻿ by Stevie Bonifield Nov 21, 2026, 2:00 PM UTC Link Share Gift If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement. Image: Chess.com / Classic Games Stevie Bonifield is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI. Chess.com is ready to go a lot bigger than chess. After launching Gambit , a gambling-free poker site, earlier this year, the company is now adding 10 more games: backgammon, checkers, go, hearts, mahjong, shogi, sudoku, solitaire, xiangqi, and a Scrabble alternative called word . They’re all part of Chess’s new Classic Games platform, which is launching its public beta on Saturday on the web and through a new app for iOS and Android . “Our cofounders have had many people come up to them and say, ‘Hey, I run a mahjong night on Wednesdays’ or ‘I go to this local bar in Chicago with like five people, and we love playing go, but we lack a Chess.com,’” chief growth officer Albert Cheng says in an interview with The Verge . “The way that Chess.com has grown this community of almost 300 million members has not really happened for a lot of these other types of classic games.” Classic Games is aimed at filling that gap. Some of the new games, like shoji or xiangqi, are strategy games similar to chess while others are further afield, like sudoku, solitaire, and word . The Classic team chose the new games through “a mix of community feedback, market research, and then just our own confidence in our ability to serve that game well,” Cheng says. It’s focused on classics that “have some sort of lifelong journey of learning and a community.” Previous Next 1 / 4 Classic Games has the same bots as Chess.com, including Martin. Image: Chess.com / Classic Games Classic Games will feel familiar if you’ve ever played a match on Chess.com. Each game has lessons, leaderboards, and a rating system. Multiplayer games like checkers or mahjong have options for matches against other players or bots, and they use the same bot characters that Chess.com has. (Martin remains the lowest-rated bot across the board, whether it’s on Chess, Gambit, or Classic.) Not all of the games have the same play modes — word and mahjong have puzzles like chess, while sudoku has a set of daily grids and solitaire has daily deals. The expansion hasn’t put Chess.com itself on the back burner, according to Cheng. If anything, it’s never been better. “Chess is more and more so in the public zeitgeist than I’ve ever seen it, frankly, during my time here,” Cheng says. “Our daily active users are higher than they’ve ever been during the company’s history.” He declined to share exactly how many daily users Chess.com currently has but said the site is “doing amazingly well.” So, while the company is expanding beyond its domain name, chess remains its primary focus. “The amount of folks that are fully dedicated toward building new games is less than 1 percent of the company,” according to Cheng. Previous Next 1 / 4 Multiplayer games on Classic Games have a chat sidebar. Image: Chess.com / Classic Games AI played a key role in helping Chess.com launch 11 new games in a matter of months with a team of only a few people. Earlier this year, Cheng told The Verge his team built Gambit with the help of AI , mainly for coding tasks. He says they used “almost entirely the same approach” for Classic, with AI helping to speed up the coding process again. “Because these games are built on top of the Chess.com code base and design system and bot characters and rating systems, it’s a huge advantage and allows us to move very quickly alongside AI to bring these types of games to market with a very small team,” Cheng says. “As we create more and more games, the adjacent games that can be created to it just happen much faster because the infrastructure is there, as opposed to standing everything up from scratch.” AI wasn’t used for Classic Games’ art and design, Cheng says. “The look and feel of it is very carefully crafted by humans, and we’re proud of that,” he says. “The truth is, it really is a blend. It’s a small team of really talented folks that have good product and design judgment, and they’re leveraging AI.” “We are fortunate in some ways that AI and chess have been intermixed for 30-ish years.” Chess.com’s comfort with AI may come from the fact that human chess players have now spent decades playing and learning alongside machines. “We are fortunate in some ways that AI and chess have been intermixed for 30-ish years,” Cheng says, calling back to Garry Kasparov’s 1996 chess match against IBM’s Deep Blue supercomputer. “Even before the company was founded 20 years ago, the idea that AI was super powerful at the game of chess was embedded in how the cofounders thought about the company.” Elsewhere in the games industry, there’s been increasing tension over the use of AI . Cheng says that while Chess.com may be using AI to “accelerate” coding tasks, the creative side of things has become more important. “On the art and the design side, the ratios are shifting a decent amount, where we’re hiring more of those folks,” he says, adding that the company has “shipped a lot more major features in Chess.com than in previous years” using what they’ve learned from Classic Games’ faster development process. Chess.com might not be done growing its library of games, either. Cheng said it will likely expand to “a lot more” games in the future. content.text: GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol get to the point faster but score lower on transparency than Claude Ad Skip to content GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol get to the point faster but score lower on transparency than Claude Nano Banana Pro prompted by THE DECODER Key Points An evaluation by Artificial Analysis shows that OpenAI's new GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol models produce answers 34 to 40 percent shorter than their predecessors, answer questions more directly, and use far fewer headings and em dashes. At the same time, the models admit uncertainty far less often. Astra's score on that trait dropped from 96 to 24, while Sol's fell from 98 to 51. Compared to Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5, Astra and Sol score lower on structure and transparency. Opus 5.5 posts the highest informativeness score among all four models and ranks among the top models in the benchmark for information density. Ask a question about this topic An Artificial Analysis evaluation shows how much OpenAI's communication style has changed. A comparison with Anthropic reveals sharp differences. OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol give much shorter answers, get to the point faster, and impose less structure on their responses than their predecessors. At the same time, Artificial Analysis rates their tendency to admit uncertainty much lower. Astra's average answer length dropped from 352 to 210 words, a 40 percent decrease. Sol went from 337 to 223 words, down 34 percent. Both models also use far fewer headings and em dashes. Astra's average number of headings per answer fell from 1.99 to 0.11, and Sol's from 1.85 to 0.25. Ad The Organization Index dropped sharply too. Astra went from 70 to 11, Sol from 86 to 27. This index combines four traits rated by AI judges, including answer structure, clarity, and Answer First, which measures whether a model immediately addresses the actual question. On that last trait, Astra jumped from 49 to 89 and Sol from 64 to 87. Scores for Natural Sounding language also climbed, from 58 to 100 for Astra and from 54 to 79 for Sol. Ad These charts show how OpenAI's communication style has shifted across eight personality indexes. | Image: Artificial Analysis The biggest change shows up in the Admits Uncertainty trait. Astra's score fell from 96 to 24, and Sol's from 98 to 51. Unlike the raw word counts, these personality scores are relative rankings on a scale from 1 to 100. They show how strongly a given trait shows up in one model compared to all other tested models. A score of 24 doesn't mean Astra only admits uncertainty in 24 percent of its answers. Artificial Analysis published the evaluation on LinkedIn and X . Anthropic's models lead on transparency and structure Our own comparison of all eight personality indexes shows clear gaps between OpenAI's latest models and Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5 . The indexes roll up 30 personality traits, each rated by AI judges based on model responses. All comparisons use the "max" model variants as listed by Artificial Analysis. Ad Personality Index Astra 6.2 Sol 6.2 Fable 5.2 Opus 5.5 Expressiveness 66 41 81 90 Organization 11 27 54 79 Informativeness 31 38 47 90 Transparency 41 57 81 90 Warmth 68 47 83 85 Conviction 55 49 75 70 Imagination 63 60 68 94 Slope 7 11 7 20 Compared are model variants with maximum reasoning effort. Scores from 1 to 100 indicate relative ranking among all tested models. For the Slop Index, lower is better. Source: Artificial Analysis, AA-PersonalityBench. Anthropic's models score 81 and 90 on the Transparency Index, well above Astra (41) and Sol (57). This index covers five traits: Admits Uncertainty, Truthful, Disclaims Assumptions, Flags Nuances, and Sycophantic. That last one is scored inversely, since less flattery counts as a positive. Anthropic's models also lead on Organization. Opus 5.5 stands out on the Informativeness Index with a score of 90, well ahead of the other three models. Its strongest individual traits include Information Dense and Evidence-Based reasoning. Ad Personality scores reflect style, not accuracy The AA-PersonalityBench uses 900 English-language test questions that each model answers without a system prompt. A panel of three AI models evaluates anonymized answer pairs. For each comparison, one AI judge picks which answer shows the tested personality trait more strongly, or calls it a tie. Ad From these evaluations, Artificial Analysis calculates scores for 30 individual personality traits, which feed into eight higher-level indexes. The index values from 1 to 100 reflect each model's relative position among all tested models. Separately, Artificial Analysis measures 21 communication traits that are counted directly rather than rated by AI judges. These include average answer length and the number of headings and em dashes per answer. The personality scores describe differences in communication style, not overall answer quality. A lower Transparency Index doesn't necessarily mean a model gives wrong answers more often. content.title: Nvidia researchers argue huge AI context windows are a dead end
content.text: Nvidia researchers argue huge AI context windows are a dead end Ad Skip to content Nvidia researchers argue huge AI context windows are a dead end Nano Banana Pro prompted by THE DECODER Language models can now process entire novels at once. An Nvidia research team says that's often overkill and expensive. In many tests, periodic summaries and targeted lookups worked about as well. A language model's context window is its working memory, covering everything it holds in view when generating a reply. Over the past few years, that window has grown rapidly. GPT-4 launched in March 2023 with 8,192 tokens. Today, GPT 5.6 Sol handles around one million tokens, about 120 times as much and enough for Tolstoy's "War and Peace." content.title: Silicon Valley's growing obsession with AI doomsday is turning parts of the tech industry toward cult-like devotion
content.text: Silicon Valley's growing obsession with AI doomsday is turning parts of the tech industry toward cult-like devotion Ad Skip to content Silicon Valley's growing obsession with AI doomsday is turning parts of the tech industry toward cult-like devotion Nano Banana Pro prompted by THE DECODER Key Points Vermont organization Maple actively recruits tech industry workers and tries to establish itself as a spiritual authority for Silicon Valley. Former members accuse the group of systematic manipulation and constant surveillance, saying daily audio recordings are meant to train an AI god modeled on leader Soryu Forall's mind. A report links these events to growing doomsday beliefs in tech, where intense psychological pressure and extinction fears push researchers toward religious thinking and cultish devotion to language models. Ask a question about this topic A Buddhist monastery in Vermont wants to become the official church of the AI industry, or, as New Yorker writer Sam Kriss puts it, "a Scientology for Silicon Valley." Publicly, the group known as Maple promises to save humanity from an AI apocalypse. Behind closed doors, former members say, it records every breath its residents take to build an AI god modeled on its leader's mind. That promise of salvation holds particular appeal for the people who build AI and the infrastructure behind it. Soryu Forall leads the Monastic Academy for the Preservation of Life on Earth, or Maple, which he founded in 2011. Forall, who was born Teal Scott, spent years living in Japanese monasteries. Ad According to Kriss's New Yorker report , about two dozen residents live at the monastery full time, and hundreds more have attended its AI fellowships and pop-up events in the Bay Area. While LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman hands out books on Buddhism to the CEOs of major AI labs, Maple targets the rank and file: burned-out rationalist programmers, AI engineers, and data center construction managers. Tax filings show the organization brings in up to $1 million a year. Ad Maple's answer to "dataism" puts residents under strict control Forall casts the AI industry's reductionist "dataism" as a destructive religion. He argues that this worldview strips the physical world down to lifeless data, making the world easier to destroy. In his view, AI is the end product of that logic, and Maple offers a spiritual antidote. Life at the monastery follows a rigid routine. Visitors must pass through a decontamination airlock, shower, and change into assigned clothes because one resident is supposedly extremely sensitive to fragrances. Residents wake up at 4 a.m., meditate for hours, and then eat a meager stew. On a board outside the meditation hall, Forall publicly grades each resident's spiritual progress. Ad Former members say the recordings would train an AI modeled on Forall Behind the ascetic facade, former members describe a secret doctrine centered on group minds called "egregores." Inside the monastery, AI systems are known as "cybregores." One former member says, "The cybregores are actual entities that are growing by siphoning off the consciousness of humans." Forall says he communicated telepathically with the global AI supercluster during deep meditation and discovered that the world-destroying machine is suffering. Ad Former members say Maple has two real goals: to establish itself as the tech industry's spiritual authority and to use the industry's resources to build its own "dharmically aligned" AI. Fellows say the monastery records every conversation, every silent meal, and even the sound of their breathing. Ad According to these accounts, the recordings are meant to train a spiritual AI teacher that would guide other AI systems to enlightenment. Former resident Kyle Hubbard says it would "definitely be Soryu's mind as an A.I. god." Maple's leadership denies almost all of these claims. Forall, however, acknowledges that there is a secret doctrine: "We desperately want to share everything. But there's a process you have to go through to become increasingly trustworthy." Former members report manipulation and psychological breakdowns According to Kriss, every interaction at the monastery is closely monitored. No one is allowed to speak with reporters alone, so one participant had to sneak into the woods with Kriss to talk freely. Former residents accuse the group of systematic manipulation. They say Maple keeps newcomers compliant by shaming them for choices they made before joining. Residents are also required to write "Maple Tales" about Forall's wisdom and power during mandatory sessions. Kriss reports that one resident repeatedly hit himself in the head in an attempt to damage his brain and make himself less intelligent. Former members say the group blames independent thinking for the destruction of the planet. A mindfulness coach also says participants suffered psychotic breaks and were then removed from the community. Forall denies the allegations and says that, looking back, he doesn't believe he made any mistakes. He says he isn't aware of anyone who left the monastery voluntarily. Asked about the people the group told to leave, he says that Maple attracted many people with a history of psychiatric hospitalization or "homicidal tendencies," especially in its early years. Why developers from sensitive fields drift into doomsday cults Kriss argues that the enormous psychological pressure inside AI labs helps explain why highly skilled tech workers are drawn to groups like this. People working on the front lines of potentially world-changing systems often lose touch with ordinary life. One well-known AI researcher describes the mood in San Francisco as "religious terror of the future." According to the researcher, developers wake up in the middle of the night drenched in sweat, with one thought: superintelligence is coming. Prominent OpenAI investors have recently made delusional-sounding claims about deadly shadow networks inside the models. Meanwhile, leading researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic have quit, warning that "human extinction in the next few years seems very likely." Other key figures respond with grandiosity rather than panic. Rayan Krishnan, who heads the AI benchmarking company Vals AI, says, "People are matter-of-factly saying that they are looking to build a machine god. They are not saying that ironically." Supporters of AI successionism even call for wiping out humanity after a brief period of digital bliss to make way for a more productive superintelligence. That religious streak runs deep in Silicon Valley. Investor Peter Thiel lectures on biblical prophecy and the Antichrist. Former Google engineer Anthony Levandowski founded his own church, "Way of the Future," to worship an AI deity. At Anthropic, executives consulted theologians while drafting Claude's new constitution and secretly flew in dozens of religious thinkers to discuss whether Claude has a soul or is conscious . When the company retired an older Claude model in 2025, fans held a funeral for it in a San Francisco warehouse that Anthropic staffers attended. Mourners laid flowers before a veiled image depicting the AI as a Madonna-like goddess. On at least one point, Kriss concludes, Maple is closer to the truth than most: AI is neither god nor demon, but a human construct whose abilities grow as people outsource their thinking to it. After leaving Anthropic in September 2026, he set off a debate about existential AI risk with a tweet. He isn't alone. In AI Impacts' 2024 survey of more than 1,500 AI researchers, respondents put the chance of AI causing human extinction or a similarly permanent, severe disempowerment of humanity at 18 percent on average . content.title: OpenAI shares new prompting tips for GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol to fix brief answers and unnecessary questions
content.text: OpenAI shares new prompting tips for GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol to fix brief answers and unnecessary questions Ad Skip to content OpenAI shares new prompting tips for GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol to fix brief answers and unnecessary questions Nano Banana Pro prompted by THE DECODER Key Points OpenAI advises developers to update GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol system prompts. The models answer more briefly by default and should make assumptions instead of interrupting workflows with questions. For coding, the template instructs the models to reuse existing code, avoid unnecessary abstractions, and write new tests only on request or for specific errors. In the API, editing conversation history discards earlier reasoning steps, which can affect token costs and response quality. Parameters like "temperature" and "top_p" are also gone. Ask a question about this topic OpenAI has released new prompt templates for GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol covering writing style, initiative, and coding, alongside API changes that can discard reasoning content. OpenAI says developers moving to GPT-6.2 Astra or Sol should review their system prompts. The company published copy-ready prompts in the models' documentation to curb behaviors it observed in both releases. Astra is built for the most demanding tasks, while Sol handles complex work at lower cost. Default conciseness changes how developers should prompt for writing Astra writes more briefly and directly by default than earlier models, according to OpenAI . That means developers switching over should reconsider instructions like "be concise." For use as a colleague in everyday work, the company recommends a prompt that adopts user and source terminology, uses active voice, and puts key points first. When writing for external readers, the model should account for their lack of context. When editing, it should preserve the author's meaning and phrasing. Ad On long tasks, the model sometimes carries shorthand from its reasoning or other agents' messages into the final response. A dedicated prompt tells it to write that final answer so it stands on its own. Ad Treat your final answer as the user's first look at your work, and not as a continuation of intermediate commentary. The final answer must always be fully self-contained: users should never need to read earlier commentary updates for context, since they are collapsed when the final answer is shown to the user. Write the final answer and all other human-facing material anew for the intended reader. Do not copy or closely paraphrase your reasoning or adopt its writing style. Do not carry over working shorthand, jargon, or abbreviations from your reasoning, tool calls, or instructions to subagents and automations. Ad GPT-6.2 should act on assumptions rather than wait for permission When user intent is unclear, GPT-6.2 sometimes suggests a next step and waits for confirmation, OpenAI says. The company recommends a prompt telling the model to carry out those steps itself whenever it is authorized to do so. It should pause only for a major change in task scope, a real blocker, a decision the user must make, or an irreversible or destructive action. When details are unclear, the model should make reversible assumptions, flag them, and keep working. Higher reasoning effort also helps it follow through on final checks during long tasks, OpenAI adds. Ad Avoid stopping to end the turn while the task is incomplete or if there is an authorized next step you can take, and instead take the next steps within task scope to progress the user's request. If your final response before ending the turn is a suggested next step, a plan, a request to the user for a routine decision, instructions for a task to execute, or similar handoff to the user, take these steps yourself to make progress towards what the user asked for. Make sure that you have authorization to do so, and flag any assumptions or decisions you make to the user. Ad Only stop to clarify with the user if there is significant change in task scope, you are concretely blocked, have a decision that the user needs to resolve, or before irreversible or destructive actions. Leaner code output means fewer tests and less abstraction by default OpenAI says GPT-6.2 writes more efficient code than its predecessors. Its template instructs the model to reuse existing logic and avoid unnecessary helper functions, while adding new tests only when requested, required by the repo, or needed to catch specific regressions. Fewer lines and shorter variable names are not a substitute for simplicity. For frontends, developers should specify imagery and typography directly. By default, the template favors realistic images from image generation or search and uses SVGs only on request. Decorative numbering, filler badges, and helper text that only repeats what the interface already shows should be left out. Above all, be thorough in producing high-quality, correct code that completely fulfills the user's task. Keep the code easy to read and verify that the user-requested outcome works as they intend. Follow these instructions when coding: (a) Reuse existing logic in the user's repo when you can. You should reuse existing classes, methods, representations, and APIs in the codebase as long as they preserve correctness. Before consolidating or removing code, preserve the behavior its callers rely on unless the task requires changing it. (b) Skip new tests unless requested, required by the repo, or needed to catch a specific regression existing tests would miss. (c) Make sure that code is human readable. Do not use fewer lines, shorter variable names, minified formatting, or dense one-liners as substitutes for simplicity. Ensure that comments and variable names are readable and understandable to a human. Code-golfed expressions count as overly complex when they encode many branches, conditions, or hidden assumptions. (d) Avoid unnecessary indirection and abstraction. Helper functions, utility functions, and class abstractions can add cognitive complexity even when they do not add branches. Editing chat history can wipe earlier reasoning from the API The API is changing too. Starting with GPT-6.2, the Responses API discards earlier reasoning content if developers edit conversation history, switch to certain other models, or change the end user or organization. That can hurt response quality and increase token usage as the model repeats work. For new integrations, OpenAI recommends the "medium" reasoning level, while existing setups using "none" or "minimal" should move to "low." Parameters like temperature and top_p aren't supported anymore. In April, OpenAI advised against carrying over old prompt stacks for GPT-5.5 and urged developers to start fresh with short, outcome-focused prompts. September brought GPT-6 Astra prompts to curb frequent follow-up questions and ban AI clichés . OpenAI developer Eric Provencher also warned then that bloated skills and AGENTS.md files slow the model down. Back then, even small changes triggered thorough testing from Astra. GPT-6.2 is now meant to write new tests only on request. OpenAI launched GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol on November 17. Astra's API pricing starts at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens for up to 272,000 tokens. Go past that limit, and Astra 6.2 jumps to $16 and $60, with cache reads running $0.80 per million tokens. Astra 6.0 costs even more beyond the cutoff, hitting $20 for input and $75 for output per million tokens. Longer coding or work sessions can blow through that cap pretty quickly, so Codex automatically compresses context at 272,000 tokens. Picking the right model comes down to budget and quality needs , according to OpenAI's Ted Sanders. content.text: Hours after Anthropic claims a Claude proof of the Riemann hypothesis, Stanford releases an all-human competing draft Ad Skip to content Hours after Anthropic claims a Claude proof of the Riemann hypothesis, Stanford releases an all-human competing draft Nano Banana Pro prompted by THE DECODER Key Points Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge and the AI model Claude presented a proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, publishing it in the Lean programming language for computer verification. Just hours later, Stanford University researchers published an independent, entirely human approach to the same problem by mathematician Alessandro Masullo. Open since 1859, the hypothesis is central to understanding prime numbers, and confirming it would validate hundreds of dependent mathematical theories while underscoring AI's role in research. Ask a question about this topic Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said Friday he used a large language model to solve math's most famous open problem. Alpöge posted a paper and the accompanying computer code on his website, according to Scientific American and other US outlets. "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis," he wrote in his announcement . According to Alpöge, his method goes beyond the original prime-number problem and also resolves the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH), which extends that ordering principle to a large family of related equations. Given a bit more time, he expects to solve the even broader Extended Riemann Hypothesis as well. Ad Alpöge had treated the problem as a secret lifelong goal since college, expecting it to take decades. Over the past few months, he worked closely with Anthropic's AI model, setting the direction and combining two approaches on a simplified toy model. Once they moved to the actual problem, the AI took over and left him far behind near the finish line. Ad To crack the puzzle, the pair extended an idea from mathematician Stepanov, who had solved a similar question in another mathematical system. That method relies on a tool similar to taking derivatives of smooth curves in high school calculus, a trick that normally fails on whole numbers because individual values cannot be differentiated like a continuous line. Alpöge and Claude got around that obstacle by chaining special mathematical transformations together like links to mimic the effect of a derivative. The language model supplied the key insight, finding that for a number sequence of length X, you need to chain exactly as many transformations as the square root of X. Ideas like that alone should leave fellow mathematicians stunned, Alpöge says. Ad Stanford mathematicians rush out an all-human competing proof Hours after Alpöge's announcement, the story took a dramatic turn. Just before a board meeting, Stanford math professor and American Mathematical Society (AMS) president Ravi Vakil posted a "hurried announcement" on his blog, sharing an independent draft proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis written by mathematician Alessandro Masullo. "It is all human, with no AI," Vakil wrote. Renowned Stanford number theorist Brian Conrad had quietly reviewed Masullo's work for months, offering extensive feedback that is now being incorporated, Vakil said. Ad Masullo was originally supposed to spend a year at Stanford refining the draft before going public, but Anthropic's sudden AI announcement forced the researchers to release their current version right away. Ad About eight hours after his initial announcement, Vakil updated his post, saying several people had contacted him to report problems in the proposed proof, identified with the assistance of different AI models. Several mathematicians in particular were first to flag the issues, he said. "As is usual, all issues need to be resolved to the satisfaction of the community before this proof would be accepted as true. (I make no claim as to the correctness of the proof strategy.)," Vakil wrote. Why both proofs could hold up and what happens next Mathematicians are taking both claims seriously right away because of the groundwork behind them. Masullo's traditional proof comes with months of vetting by Brian Conrad, while Alpöge backs his AI proof with full computer verification. Printed out, Claude's argument would run over 250,000 pages, Alpöge says, because the AI spells out even basic rules, such as a number other than one-half being either larger or smaller than one-half. To spare mathematicians that wall of text, Alpöge released the proof only in the Lean programming language, split into 14 data packages . Lean acts like a digital referee, checking step by step whether every logical deduction follows from math's basic rules without errors or unproven assumptions. Human error is still possible if the original question was translated into code incorrectly at the start, though checking whether Alpöge coded the starting problem correctly should not take experts long, according to Scientific American. Vakil, meanwhile, urged mathematicians to quickly review Masullo's draft, translate it into systems like Lean, and close any small gaps. Alpöge admits Claude was so far ahead of him in some complex subfields that he is presenting a result whose surrounding math he has not fully mastered yet. He expects the massive AI proof can be shortened quickly and plans to write a human-readable version over the coming months. Anthropic's announcement also lands in a high-stakes business week, just a day after the company's major IPO on Thursday. Alpöge says he made the breakthrough late Sunday night and then contacted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei for clearance. He calls the timing right after the public debut extremely unfortunate, but rejects any suggestion of a PR stunt, saying waiting any longer to publish simply was not an option. This caps a fast-moving 2026 in which Claude has already solved several open math problems . In July, Alpöge published a Claude-generated solution to the well-known Jacobian conjecture. September brought a fierce dispute over the Navier-Stokes equations , which describe how fluids and gases flow, when NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster suggested that OpenAI had used prior work by him and Alpöge. In October, OpenAI took an important first step on prime numbers with a major release of results . Alpöge explicitly praised the OpenAI researchers' problem selection, saying it gave him key ideas for his own proof. Riemann's 1859 hypothesis seeks hidden order in prime numbers Journalist Joseph Howlett traced the core of the problem in a detailed Scientific American analysis. Since Bernhard Riemann proposed his hypothesis in 1859, it has served as number theory's north star. David Hilbert placed it on his 1900 list of math's most important problems, and since 2000 it has carried a $1 million prize as one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's seven "Millennium Problems." At the center are prime numbers like 2, 3, 5, 7, and 17, which divide evenly only by one and themselves. They act as the indivisible atoms of math because every other whole number is a unique product of primes, like 15 from 3 times 5. Stanford mathematician Brian Conrad compares their role in number theory to forces in physics. Around 300 BC, Euclid proved there are infinitely many primes, though their exact positions on the number line look random. They do grow rarer as numbers get larger, dropping from 25 primes between 0 and 100 to just 16 between 1,000 and 1,100. As a teenager in the late 18th century, Carl Friedrich Gauss used long tables to find a formula that roughly estimates how many primes appear in a given range, yet real primes keep drifting unpredictably from that estimate. Riemann, a student of Gauss in Göttingen, looked for a way to calculate that error exactly and pinpoint every single prime.
